exam: A 6‑year‑old with sickle cell disease presents with chest pain and SpO2 92 % – what immediate investigation and why? — Obtain a chest X‑ray to rule out acute chest syndrome; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics if infection suspected.
A pregnant woman in a rural clinic has Hb 7 g/dL but no lab for ferritin – how do you decide on iron therapy? — Use WHO anemia grading; start oral iron and arrange follow‑up CBC in 4 weeks.
A patient with severe malaria is anaemic (Hb 6 g/dL) – when is transfusion indicated? — Transfuse if Hb < 7 g/dL or if there are signs of cardiac compromise.
You suspect carbon monoxide poisoning but pulse oximeter reads 98 % – what test confirms the diagnosis? — Obtain a CO‑oximeter or ABG with COHb level; treat with high‑flow O2 regardless.

In a patient with HIV, anemia persists despite iron – what is the next step? — Check serum ferritin and consider anemia of chronic disease; treat underlying HIV and consider erythropoietin if indicated.

A child with chronic cough and pallor is found to have Hb 9 g/dL – which cause is most likely in this setting? — Chronic infection (TB) or helminthic disease causing anemia of chronic disease; investigate with sputum microscopy and stool exam.
Why is hydroxyurea preferred over frequent transfusions in severe sickle cell disease? — It reduces sickling frequency, lowering transfusion‑related infection risk and iron overload.
A patient on antiretroviral therapy develops macrocytic anemia – which drug is most likely responsible? — Zidovudine (AZT) can cause bone‑marrow suppression leading to macrocytosis.
ai.title: Oxygen Transport Disorders
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Oxygen transport depends on hemoglobin, red cell mass and cardiac output. Disruption can cause tissue hypoxia, anemia, or toxic inhibition, especially in low‑resource settings where common infections and hemoglobinopathies prevail.

b: Measure hemoglobin concentration and hematocrit
Assess oxygen saturation (SpO2) and arterial blood gases (ABG) when available
Look for clinical signs of tissue hypoxia (tachypnea, confusion, cyanosis)
sections.p: Oxygen transport disorders encompass any condition that reduces the amount of oxygen reaching tissues, including anemia, hemoglobinopathies, cardiac failure, and toxic inhibition of hemoglobin.

b: Mild: Hb 10‑12 g/dL, SpO2 ≥ 94 % and no organ dysfunction
Moderate: Hb 8‑9.9 g/dL, SpO2 90‑93 % or mild dyspnoea
Severe: Hb < 8 g/dL, SpO2 < 90 % or signs of shock, altered mental status
sections.p: Severity is graded by hemoglobin level, oxygen saturation, and presence of end‑organ dysfunction.

HIV‑related marrow suppression
Tuberculosis‑associated anemia of chronic disease
Carbon monoxide poisoning (if indoor smoke exposure)

sections.p: Patients present with fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, pallor, tachycardia, and in severe cases, confusion or chest pain.

b: Iron supplementation for iron‑deficiency (oral ferrous sulfate preferred; avoid IV iron if facilities limited)
Folate or vitamin B12 for macrocytic anemia
Hydroxyurea for severe sickle cell disease (if available) – reduces sickling

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then support oxygen delivery.
